4.2 Emergency Matters

If a client reports an imminent hearing, eviction, or other time-sensitive legal action, the intake coordinator must flag the file as "EXPEDITED" and notify a supervising attorney within 2 hours. Expedited matters bypass the standard waiting period but still require a complete conflict check before any substantive work begins.

4.3 Telephone Screening Script

All telephone intake should follow the approved screening script (Appendix A). The script is designed to gather the minimum information needed to determine whether the matter falls within BLAC's priority areas. Do not ask for detailed factual narratives during the initial call; that information is collected during the full intake interview.

5. CONFLICT CHECK

5.1 Requirement

No case may be opened, and no substantive legal advice may be given, until a conflict check has been completed. The conflict check must be run against the BLAC case management system and the regional pro bono conflict database.

5.2 Procedure

1. Enter the client's full name, date of birth, and any known aliases into the conflict check module.
2. Also enter the names of any adverse parties, if known.
3. Review the results for any matches against current or former BLAC clients.
4. If a potential conflict is identified, escalate to the supervising attorney immediately. Do not proceed with intake until the conflict is resolved in writing.

5.3 Timing

The conflict check must be completed within 2 business days of the initial contact. For expedited matters, it must be completed the same day.

6. ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION

6.1 General Eligibility Criteria

To be eligible for BLAC services, a client must meet all of the following criteria:

Intake Form 2023 has_version v3. Record status: historical.

- Reside in Bridgeport, Fairfield, or New Haven County
- Have income at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (see Appendix B for current income chart)
- Have a legal problem that falls within one of BLAC's priority areas (housing, family law, public benefits, consumer protection, or immigration)
- Not be represented by another attorney on the same matter

6.2 Exceptions

The Executive Director or Managing Attorney may grant an exception to the income or geographic criteria in exceptional circumstances. Exceptions must be documented in writing and placed in the client file.

6.3 Priority Areas

The following matters receive priority for intake:

- Eviction defense and housing habitability
- Protection orders and family violence matters
- Denial or termination of SNAP, Medicaid, or TANF benefits
- Immigration matters for victims of crime (U visa, VAWA)
- Foreclosure prevention

Matters outside these priority areas may be accepted on a case-by-case basis if capacity exists, or referred to partner organizations.

7. DOCUMENTATION COLLECTION AND VERIFICATION

7.1 Required Documents

The following documents must be collected before a case is formally opened:

- Government-issued photo identification (driver's license, state ID, passport, or consular ID)
- Proof of income for all household members (pay stubs, benefit award letters, tax returns, or a signed statement if no documentation is available)
- Proof of address (utility bill, lease agreement, or mail addressed to the client)
- Any documents relevant to the legal matter (lease, court filings, benefit denial letters, etc.)

7.2 Document Handling

Original documents must never be kept in the client file. Staff should make copies or scan all documents and return originals to the client immediately. Scanned documents must be uploaded to the case management system within 3 business days of receipt.

7.3 Verification
8. INTAKE FORM VERSIONS AND EFFECTIVE DATES

The Bridgeport Legal Aid Collaborative uses a standardized intake form to collect client information, assess eligibility, and document consent to representation. The form has been revised several times to reflect changes in law, technology, and internal procedure. This section describes the current form and the history of prior versions. Staff must always use the current version posted on the shared drive under Forms > Intake, and must never use a superseded version to open a new matter.

8.1 Current Version: Intake Form 2024 v4

Intake Form 2024 has_version v4. Record status: current. This is the only version that may be used for new intakes as of the effective date of this manual. The form is available in English and Spanish. If a client requires interpretation in another language, staff should request interpreter services before beginning the intake interview. Do not use a family member or friend as an interpreter unless the client insists and the situation is urgent; document the circumstances in the case notes.

The v4 form consists of five sections: (A) Client Information, (B) Household and Income, (C) Legal Problem Description, (D) Conflict Check and Authorizations, and (E) Certification and Review. A summary of key fields is provided below, followed by the substantive changes from v3.

8.1.1 Section A – Client Information

This section collects basic identifying information: full legal name, date of birth, social security number (optional), current address, mailing address if different, phone number, email address, and preferred language. Clients are not required to provide a social security number. If the client declines, leave the field blank and do not mark the form as incomplete. The address field must be completed with a physical address. A P.O. Box alone is not sufficient for eligibility purposes unless the client certifies they are unhoused, in which case staff should complete the Housing Status field in Section C.

New to v4: a checkbox for “Client prefers to receive documents by email” and a second checkbox for “Client consents to text message reminders.” These checkboxes are informational only. Staff should verify that the client can reliably access email or text messages before relying on those methods for service of documents. If the client cannot, use U.S. mail as the default method.

8.1.2 Section B – Household and Income

This section captures the client’s household size, the income of each household member, and the source of that income (employment, SNAP, SSI/SSDI, unemployment, child support, pension, or “other” with a written description). The form includes a chart where each household member is listed by first name and relationship. Staff must ask about income from all sources, including informal or under-the-table work. Clients are asked to estimate monthly income if they do not have exact figures. The form includes a field for “Total Monthly Household Income” and a field for “Number of Dependents Under 18.”

Also new to v4: a question asking whether any household member has experienced a change in income in the last 30 days, with a yes/no checkbox and a short explanation field. This is intended to capture recent job loss or benefit termination that may affect eligibility or urgency.

8.1.3 Section C – Legal Problem Description

This section asks the client to describe their legal problem in their own words. Staff should write the client’s description as close to verbatim as possible, using quotation marks if the client’s own words are recorded. The form then asks staff to select the primary legal category from a dropdown list: Housing, Family Law, Public Benefits, Consumer Protection, Immigration, or Other. If “Other” is selected, a text field appears for a written description. Staff should select only one primary category. If the matter spans multiple categories, note the secondary category in the case notes.

**8. Intake Procedures (continued)**

**8.1.4 Section D – Opposing Party and Related Parties**

Section D collects identifying information about the opposing party or parties and any related individuals (e.g., a landlord, an employer, a government agency, or a family member in a custody matter). Staff must complete this section for every intake, even if the only information available is a name. Do not leave the section blank because the client is uncertain about details; record what is known and flag missing items in the case notes.

Fields include:

- Full legal name (if known) and any aliases
- Relationship to client
- Address, phone number, and email (if available)
- Employer or agency name and address (if applicable)
- Attorney of record, if any, with bar number

For eviction matters, the opposing party will typically be the landlord or property management company. For family law matters, include the other parent or guardian. For public benefits cases, list the agency and, if known, the specific office or hearing officer.

Staff should confirm the spelling of all names and addresses with the client before entering them into the Case Management System (CMS). Incorrect opposing party information is a frequent cause of service delays and continuances.

**8.1.5 Section E – Prior Contacts and Referrals**

This section asks the client whether they have contacted any other legal services provider, private attorney, court self-help center, or government agency about the same problem. The form includes a yes/no checkbox and a text field for details. If the client answers yes, staff must record:

- The name of the provider or agency
- The date of the contact (approximate if unknown)
- The outcome, if any
- Whether the client has a pending case or active representation elsewhere

This information is used to avoid duplicate representation and to coordinate with other providers. If the client has been referred by another agency, record the referral source and any referral number or contact person. Referrals from the courthouse, hospital social workers, and community partners are common and should be noted in the referral source dropdown.

New to v4: a checkbox for “Client is currently represented by another attorney” and a separate checkbox for “Client has an upcoming court date.” These checkboxes are informational and should be completed in addition to the narrative field. If the client has an upcoming court date, staff must enter the date and court location in the case notes and flag the matter as urgent in the CMS.

**8.1.6 Section F – Urgency and Safety Concerns**

Section F is used to identify matters that require immediate attention or that involve safety risks. The form includes the following checkboxes:

- Client is homeless or at risk of homelessness
- Client has an upcoming hearing or filing deadline (within 14 days)
- Client is experiencing domestic violence or safety concerns
- Client is a minor, elderly, or has a disability that affects access to services
- Client is in removal proceedings or has a detention hearing

If any box is checked, staff must notify the intake supervisor before completing the rest of the intake. The supervisor will determine whether the matter should be expedited or referred to a specialized unit. Do not delay action on a safety concern while waiting for additional information.

The form also includes a free-text field for “Description of Urgency or Safety Concern.” Staff should write a concise but complete description, including any dates, threats, or court orders. For domestic violence matters, do not include the client’s address or phone number in this field if the client has requested confidentiality. Use the separate confidential contact form instead.

I have reviewed the intake materials and the client's documents. The client's version of events is plausible and supported by the money order receipt and the text messages. 1. Proof of payment. The money order receipt is the strongest piece of evidence. It is dated 03/01/2023, which is within the first five days of the month, and is made out to the landlord by name. The landlord has not provided any documentation showing he returned the money order or that it was not negotiable. We should request the money order's payment status from Western Union (may require a subpoena, but worth trying informally first). If the money order was never cashed, that cuts against the landlord, but it also means the client may still owe rent. We need to know.

The Case File #2023-0147 (Case 147) intake_date is 2023-03-22. Record status: historical.

2. Retaliatory eviction. The client made a written repair request (text message) on 03/15/2023, three days before the Notice to Quit was dated. Under CT law, an eviction within six months of a good-faith repair request creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation. The landlord's justification (non-payment) is disputed, so this presumption could be key. We should file the Fair Housing complaint with CT CHRO as a backstop and also consider a housing code enforcement complaint. The city's landlord registration status is also relevant — if the landlord is not registered, the eviction may be stayed until he registers.

3. Habitability. The photos show water damage and possible mold. If the ceiling leak has been ongoing and the landlord has not repaired it, the client may have a defense based on breach of the implied warranty of habitability. However, the client has continued to pay rent, so she is not in a strong position to withhold rent unless we can document the condition more thoroughly. Consider a housing inspector visit. The client should keep a log of any further water damage or mold growth.

4. Lease. Client does not have a copy. She says she signed a one-year lease in August 2022 and never received a copy. The landlord has not provided one. 5. Landlord registration. Bridgeport requires landlords to register with the city. I will check the public registry tomorrow. If the landlord is not registered, we should file a complaint with the city's housing code enforcement and note it in the answer.

If a client reports an imminent hearing, eviction, or other time-sensitive legal action, the intake coordinator must flag the file as "EXPEDITED" and notify a supervising attorney within 2 hours. 4.3 Telephone Screening Script

All telephone intake should follow the approved screening script (Appendix A). The script is designed to gather the minimum information needed to determine whether the matter falls within BLAC's priority areas. Do not ask for detailed factual narratives during the initial call; that information is collected during the full intake interview.

5. CONFLICT CHECK

5.1 Requirement

No case may be opened, and no substantive legal advice may be given, until a conflict check has been completed. The conflict check must be run against the BLAC case management system and the regional pro bono conflict database.

5.2 Procedure

1. Enter the client's full name, date of birth, and any known aliases into the conflict check module.
2. Also enter the names of any adverse parties, if known.
3. Review the results for any matches against current or former BLAC clients.
4. If a potential conflict is identified, escalate to the supervising attorney immediately. Do not proceed with intake until the conflict is resolved in writing.

5.3 Timing

The conflict check must be completed within 2 business days of the initial contact. For expedited matters, it must be completed the same day.

6.1 General Eligibility Criteria

The Executive Director or Managing Attorney may grant an exception to the income or geographic criteria in exceptional circumstances. Exceptions must be documented in writing and placed in the client file.

6.3 Priority Areas

The following matters receive priority for intake:

The following documents must be collected before a case is formally opened:

- Government-issued photo identification (driver's license, state ID, passport, or consular ID)
- Proof of income for all household members (pay stubs, benefit award letters, tax returns, or a signed statement if no documentation is available)
- Proof of address (utility bill, lease agreement, or mail addressed to the client)
- Any documents relevant to the legal matter (lease, court filings, benefit denial letters, etc.)

documents.content:
8. INTAKE FORM VERSIONS AND EFFECTIVE DATES

The Bridgeport Legal Aid Collaborative uses a standardized intake form to collect client information, assess eligibility, and document consent to representation. The form has been revised several times to reflect changes in law, technology, and internal procedure. This section describes the current form and the history of prior versions. Staff must always use the current version posted on the shared drive under Forms > Intake, and must never use a superseded version to open a new matter.

8.1 Current Version: Intake Form 2024 v4

Intake Form 2024 has_version v4. Record status: current. This is the only version that may be used for new intakes as of the effective date of this manual. The form is available in English and Spanish. If a client requires interpretation in another language, staff should request interpreter services before beginning the intake interview. Do not use a family member or friend as an interpreter unless the client insists and the situation is urgent; document the circumstances in the case notes.

The v4 form consists of five sections: (A) Client Information, (B) Household and Income, (C) Legal Problem Description, (D) Conflict Check and Authorizations, and (E) Certification and Review. A summary of key fields is provided below, followed by the substantive changes from v3.

8.1.1 Section A – Client Information

This section collects basic identifying information: full legal name, date of birth, social security number (optional), current address, mailing address if different, phone number, email address, and preferred language. Clients are not required to provide a social security number. If the client declines, leave the field blank and do not mark the form as incomplete. The address field must be completed with a physical address. A P.O. Box alone is not sufficient for eligibility purposes unless the client certifies they are unhoused, in which case staff should complete the Housing Status field in Section C.

New to v4: a checkbox for “Client prefers to receive documents by email” and a second checkbox for “Client consents to text message reminders.” These checkboxes are informational only. Staff should verify that the client can reliably access email or text messages before relying on those methods for service of documents. If the client cannot, use U.S. mail as the default method.

8.1.2 Section B – Household and Income

This section captures the client’s household size, the income of each household member, and the source of that income (employment, SNAP, SSI/SSDI, unemployment, child support, pension, or “other” with a written description). The form includes a chart where each household member is listed by first name and relationship. Staff must ask about income from all sources, including informal or under-the-table work. Clients are asked to estimate monthly income if they do not have exact figures. The form includes a field for “Total Monthly Household Income” and a field for “Number of Dependents Under 18.”

Also new to v4: a question asking whether any household member has experienced a change in income in the last 30 days, with a yes/no checkbox and a short explanation field. This is intended to capture recent job loss or benefit termination that may affect eligibility or urgency.

8.1.3 Section C – Legal Problem Description

This section asks the client to describe their legal problem in their own words. Staff should write the client’s description as close to verbatim as possible, using quotation marks if the client’s own words are recorded. The form then asks staff to select the primary legal category from a dropdown list: Housing, Family Law, Public Benefits, Consumer Protection, Immigration, or Other. If “Other” is selected, a text field appears for a written description. Staff should select only one primary category. **Intake Procedures Manual**

**8. Intake Procedures (continued)**

**8.1.4 Section D – Opposing Party and Related Parties**

Section D collects identifying information about the opposing party or parties and any related individuals (e.g., a landlord, an employer, a government agency, or a family member in a custody matter). Staff must complete this section for every intake, even if the only information available is a name. Do not leave the section blank because the client is uncertain about details; record what is known and flag missing items in the case notes.

Fields include:

- Full legal name (if known) and any aliases
- Relationship to client
- Address, phone number, and email (if available)
- Employer or agency name and address (if applicable)
- Attorney of record, if any, with bar number

For eviction matters, the opposing party will typically be the landlord or property management company. For family law matters, include the other parent or guardian. For public benefits cases, list the agency and, if known, the specific office or hearing officer.

Staff should confirm the spelling of all names and addresses with the client before entering them into the Case Management System (CMS). Incorrect opposing party information is a frequent cause of service delays and continuances.

**8.1.5 Section E – Prior Contacts and Referrals**

This section asks the client whether they have contacted any other legal services provider, private attorney, court self-help center, or government agency about the same problem. The form includes a yes/no checkbox and a text field for details. If the client answers yes, staff must record:

- The name of the provider or agency
- The date of the contact (approximate if unknown)
- The outcome, if any
- Whether the client has a pending case or active representation elsewhere

This information is used to avoid duplicate representation and to coordinate with other providers. If the client has been referred by another agency, record the referral source and any referral number or contact person. Referrals from the courthouse, hospital social workers, and community partners are common and should be noted in the referral source dropdown.

New to v4: a checkbox for “Client is currently represented by another attorney” and a separate checkbox for “Client has an upcoming court date.” These checkboxes are informational and should be completed in addition to the narrative field. If the client has an upcoming court date, staff must enter the date and court location in the case notes and flag the matter as urgent in the CMS.

**8.1.6 Section F – Urgency and Safety Concerns**

Section F is used to identify matters that require immediate attention or that involve safety risks. The form includes the following checkboxes:

- Client is homeless or at risk of homelessness
- Client has an upcoming hearing or filing deadline (within 14 days)
- Client is experiencing domestic violence or safety concerns
- Client is a minor, elderly, or has a disability that affects access to services
- Client is in removal proceedings or has a detention hearing

If any box is checked, staff must notify the intake supervisor before completing the rest of the intake. The supervisor will determine whether the matter should be expedited or referred to a specialized unit. Do not delay action on a safety concern while waiting for additional information.

The form also includes a free-text field for “Description of Urgency or Safety Concern.” Staff should write a concise but complete description, including any dates, threats, or court orders. For domestic violence matters, do not include the client’s address or phone number in this field if the client has requested confidentiality. Use the separate confidential contact form instead.

PAGE 5 — CASE MEMO (typed, from D. Reyes)

RE: Case 147 — A. Okafor v. J. Kowalski (potential eviction defense)
Date: 03/24/2023

I have reviewed the intake materials and the client's documents. The client's version of events is plausible and supported by the money order receipt and the text messages. The landlord's claim of non-receipt is suspicious given that the client offered to show the receipt on at least two occasions and the landlord did not engage.

Key issues:

1. Proof of payment. The money order receipt is the strongest piece of evidence. It is dated 03/01/2023, which is within the first five days of the month, and is made out to the landlord by name. The landlord has not provided any documentation showing he returned the money order or that it was not negotiable. We should request the money order's payment status from Western Union (may require a subpoena, but worth trying informally first). If the money order was never cashed, that cuts against the landlord, but it also means the client may still owe rent. We need to know.

The Case File #2023-0147 (Case 147) intake_date is 2023-03-22. Record status: historical.

2. Retaliatory eviction. The client made a written repair request (text message) on 03/15/2023, three days before the Notice to Quit was dated. Under CT law, an eviction within six months of a good-faith repair request creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation. The landlord's justification (non-payment) is disputed, so this presumption could be key. We should file the Fair Housing complaint with CT CHRO as a backstop and also consider a housing code enforcement complaint. The city's landlord registration status is also relevant — if the landlord is not registered, the eviction may be stayed until he registers.

3. Habitability. The photos show water damage and possible mold. If the ceiling leak has been ongoing and the landlord has not repaired it, the client may have a defense based on breach of the implied warranty of habitability. However, the client has continued to pay rent, so she is not in a strong position to withhold rent unless we can document the condition more thoroughly. Consider a housing inspector visit. The client should keep a log of any further water damage or mold growth.

4. Lease. Client does not have a copy. She says she signed a one-year lease in August 2022 and never received a copy. The landlord has not provided one. We should formally request it from the landlord's attorney or, if necessary, via discovery. If there is no written lease, the terms are month-to-month, which changes the notice period (but the Notice to Quit appears to comply with the 30-day requirement either way).

5. Landlord registration. Bridgeport requires landlords to register with the city. I will check the public registry tomorrow. If the landlord is not registered, we should file a complaint with the city's housing code enforcement and note it in the answer.

Next steps:
- Send preservation letter to landlord (or his attorney) re: money order, text messages, photos.
- Check city landlord registry.
- File CHRO complaint (retaliation) — client has been informed and is willing.
- Obtain Western Union payment status for the money order.
- Prepare draft answer to the eviction summons (expected within 2–3 weeks, based on the Notice to Quit date).

I will update the file after the registry check.

1:30 PM – Client called. She reviewed the addendum. She has one question: the addendum says "landlord will withdraw the Notice to Quit" but does it say anything about the code enforcement violation? I told her it does not, but the violation is between the landlord and the city, not her. She asked if she should get that in writing too. I told her we can ask, but it is not part of the eviction. She said she wants to ask anyway. I will have M. Chen request a separate statement.

02/21/2024 – M. Chen
3:00 PM – Sent email to R. Delgado requesting a separate written statement from the landlord that the code enforcement violation is not the client's responsibility and that the landlord will not retaliate for the client's repair requests. Not sure if he will agree, but worth asking.

02/22/2024 – D. Okafor
11:00 AM – Client called. She is ready to sign the addendum. She asked if she can pay with a money order instead of a cashier's check. I told her the landlord asked for a cashier's check. She said she can do that. I told her we will wait for M. Chen to get the separate statement from the landlord, but if he doesn't respond by tomorrow, we will proceed with the addendum as is.

02/22/2024 – M. Chen
4:45 PM – No response from R. Delgado on the separate statement. I called his office. His paralegal, J. Ortiz, answered. She said Mr. Delgado was still reviewing the request with the landlord. She said they had a question about the wording. I asked what question. She said the landlord wanted to make sure the statement would not be interpreted as an admission that the code enforcement violation was caused by the client's repair requests. I told her that is exactly what we are trying to avoid, so the statement should say the landlord will not assert that the client caused the violation and will not retaliate for the repair requests. She said she would pass that along. I told her we need a response by noon tomorrow or we will proceed with the addendum as is.

02/23/2024 – D. Okafor
9:15 AM – Client called. She is anxious. She said her neighbor told her the landlord was "telling people" she was being evicted for calling the city. I told her that is not true, and the Notice to Quit will be withdrawn once she signs the addendum. I reminded her not to discuss the case with the neighbor. She said she understands. I told her M. Chen is waiting on the landlord's response about the separate statement, and we will call her as soon as we hear.

02/23/2024 – M. Chen
11:50 AM – No response from R. Delgado by the noon deadline. I called again. J. Ortiz said Mr. Delgado was in a deposition and would not be available until after 3 PM. I told her we were proceeding with the addendum as is. She said she would let Mr. Delgado know. I emailed the client's signed copy to J. 02/23/2024 – D. Okafor
2:00 PM – Client came in to sign the addendum. She read it one more time. She asked again about the code enforcement violation. I told her the addendum does not address it, and we will follow up separately. She signed. I gave her a copy. She said she will get the cashier's check tomorrow morning. I told her the landlord has 5 days from the landlord's signature, so she has time. She left at 2:25 PM.

02/23/2024 – M. Chen
3:30 PM – Received email from R. Delgado. Okafor.

4:10 PM – Called client to tell her the separate statement is in. She was relieved. She asked if she should keep it with the addendum. I told her yes, keep them together. She said she will pick up the cashier's check tomorrow. I reminded her to make it payable to Beacon Realty LLC, not to the landlord personally. She said she remembered.

02/26/2024 – M. Chen
10:00 AM – Received confirmation from J. Ortiz that the landlord signed the addendum on 02/24/2024. She sent a scanned copy. The addendum is fully executed. I logged it in the case file. The Notice to Quit dated 02/08/2024 is withdrawn as of the landlord's signature. I emailed the client a copy of the fully executed addendum and the separate statement.

02/26/2024 – D. Okafor
